opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been tinkering with on the side. I like going to the actual data, because the conversation about AI and jobs tends to get very abstract very fast. People say "AI will take all the jobs" or "AI will create all these new jobs," and it's hard to reason about either claim without something concrete.

What I do is take something like the Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational data. There are several hundred occupations, and for each one you get how many people work in it, what they get paid, and a description of the tasks the job involves. That last part is the interesting bit, because a job isn't one atomic thing. It's a bundle of tasks. So the question isn't really "will AI replace radiologists?" It's "which of the twenty things a radiologist does in a day can be automated, and what happens to the rest of the bundle?"

So I go through those task descriptions, honestly with the help of LLMs to do the scoring, and ask how much of this is digital. Is it information in, information out? Can you do it at a computer? Does it need physical manipulation in the world, or a lot of in-person trust and accountability? A really useful first-order heuristic is that anything that is mostly manipulating bits is going to be affected much sooner than anything that requires manipulating atoms. Atoms are just a lot harder. Robotics is coming, but it's slower, it's capital-intensive, and the deployment curve looks different.

When you lay it out like that and weight it by the number of employees and wages, you get a much more textured picture than the headlines. A large fraction of knowledge work turns out to be pretty exposed, at least at the task level. Exposure isn't the same as elimination, though. Historically, when you automate part of a job, often the job just changes. People do more of the remaining parts, or demand for the output goes up because it got cheaper. My favorite example is radiology. People predicted years ago that radiologists would be obsolete, and instead we have plenty of radiologists, because reading the scan was only one part of the job and the rest is a lot of context, communication, and liability.

So I try to hold two things in mind. One, it's a spectrum, and I think "autonomy slider" is the right way to picture it. Most jobs will move gradually from "human does it with some AI help" toward "AI does most of it and the human supervises," and the speed varies a lot by profession. Two, the data is a starting point, not an oracle. These task descriptions are coarse, and the real-world friction of regulation, organizational inertia, and trust is huge and doesn't show up in a spreadsheet.

But I think it's a healthy exercise, and I'd encourage people to do it for their own job. Write down what you actually do all day, task by task, and ask yourself honestly which parts a model could do today, which in a couple of years, and which are really about being a human in the room. That tends to be more clarifying than any big macro prediction.

r001.rationale: The response uses Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational data, including employment counts and task descriptions, to assess AI’s impact across occupations, and calls the data a starting point.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes AI helping people with tasks from eliminating jobs, noting that jobs often change, and describes a spectrum from human-led work with AI help to AI-led work with human supervision.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing I keep coming back to is that jobs data is actually a pretty bad lens for this, at least at the granularity most people use it. You see these reports that go through the Bureau of Labor Statistics occupation list and score each one for "automation risk," and I just don't think that's how it works. A job isn't a unit. A job is a bundle of tasks, and the bundle is kind of arbitrary, it's a historical accident of how we organized work.

So the way I actually think about it is I try to decompose. What are the tasks inside a given profession, and for each task, what does the input-output structure look like? Is it a task where the input is fully digital and the output is fully digital and it's verifiable? Those are the ones that go first, because that's the regime where the models can get fast feedback and where you can actually iterate. Radiology is the classic example everyone brings up, and it's instructive precisely because it didn't go the way people predicted. The image reading is a very clean task, but the radiologist's job is a lot of other stuff, it's talking to the clinicians, it's the liability, it's the edge cases, it's the physical procedures. So the task got automated, or partially automated, and the job didn't disappear. It got reshaped.

The other thing is that jobs data is a lagging indicator in a way that's kind of brutal here. By the time it shows up in the employment numbers, the transition has already happened, and what you actually want to know is what's happening upstream, at the task level, inside companies. I find it more useful to look at things like, how much of a software engineer's day is now spent reviewing versus writing? That's not in any dataset, but it's the actual signal.

And I'll say, I'm a little allergic to the framing of "which professions get replaced." I think the honest answer is that almost every knowledge job gets rewritten, and the question is less about the profession and more about the person. Are you the kind of practitioner who can orchestrate these tools, verify them, catch the mistakes? Because the models are still jagged. They're superhuman at some things and weirdly bad at others, and that jaggedness is what keeps humans in the loop. The jobs data doesn't capture any of that. It just tells you the headcount.

r001.rationale: The candidate says occupation-level jobs data is a poor lens and instead recommends starting with tasks within a profession.

r002.rationale: It contrasts automated or partially automated tasks with jobs that remain and are reshaped, and describes people orchestrating and verifying models.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful thing is to break a profession down into tasks. A job title is a pretty coarse unit. A software engineer isn’t just writing code all day. They’re talking to people, figuring out what to build, debugging things, and dealing with all kinds of context that may never be written down.

So you can look at jobs data and ask: What are the activities within each occupation? Which of those could a model do, which could it help a person do, and which are still difficult? That gives you a more useful picture than saying, “This job is going away.”

But even then, exposure to AI isn’t the same as job loss. If you make some task dramatically cheaper, people might want a lot more of it. And being able to do a task in a demo is different from doing it reliably inside an organization. So I’d use that data as a map of where work could change, rather than as a direct forecast of how many jobs disappear.

r001.rationale: It uses jobs data to break occupations into activities, but does not present occupation-level employment data as the starting point.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes tasks AI can help people with from those it can do, and explains that AI exposure does not necessarily mean job loss.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful thing is to break a job down into tasks, because a job is usually a bundle of quite different activities. Some of those might be very amenable to an LLM, and some require physical presence, a lot of context, or judgment that’s difficult to evaluate.

So I’d use jobs data to understand that task composition, and then ask: where can the model help, how reliably, and how much of someone’s time does that actually represent? Being able to do one task doesn’t mean you can replace the profession. You might just make the person more productive, and then the bottleneck moves somewhere else.

And I’d be careful about translating exposure directly into job losses. If something becomes much cheaper, people may want a lot more of it. The task data gives you a starting point, but you still have to think through how the whole workflow changes.

r001.rationale: The response uses jobs data to examine task composition, but does not clearly present occupation-level employment data as the starting point for analyzing impact profession by profession.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes assistance from displacement: models may make workers more productive, and doing one task does not mean replacing the profession.
